sources.title: Conversational Agent Interventions for Mental Health Problems: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

provenance.access_note: AI-prepared paraphrase from accessible web research text; human claim review pending. Direct B-04 attempt: manual_review; web page returned HTTP 202 Claims and limitations reviewed by Nicole on 2026-09-06.
provenance.license_note: The article footer identifies CC BY 4.0 and requires attribution to He et al., JMIR 2023;25:e43862, DOI 10.2196/43862.

references.locator: Methods: Meta-analysis (short term=postintervention; long term=follow-up); Results: Study Characteristics paragraphs 1 and 6; Risk of Bias; Efficacy

claims.text: The meta-analysis included 32 randomized studies with 6089 participants. Intervention durations were 0–4 weeks (11 studies), 5–8 weeks (10), or more than 9 weeks (11). Eight studies were rated low risk of bias, 11 some risk, and 13 high risk.

At postintervention—the review's short-term endpoint—depressive symptoms improved versus controls (Hedges g 0.29, 95% CI 0.20–0.38). The result must be read with the review's risk-of-bias distribution: 8 low-risk, 11 some-risk, and 13 high-risk studies.

Long-term results were follow-up measurements rather than postintervention measurements: 17 studies had no follow-up, 7 followed participants for 0–8 weeks, and 8 for 9 weeks or longer. Most long-term mental-health outcomes were not statistically significant, and the review rated 8 studies low risk, 11 some risk, and 13 high risk of bias.

limitations.text: Only eight studies were judged at low risk of bias; eleven had some risk and thirteen high risk.
The synthesis covers different agent types, populations and comparators. It cannot establish universal suitability.

references.locator: Plain-language summary: What studies are included?; What are the main findings?; How up-to-date is this EGM?

claims.text: Searches covered studies published only through May 2021; at the September 2026 review this evidence map is more than five years out of date. The map contains 200 articles: 97 systematic reviews and 103 primary studies. Most evidence comes from high-income settings and none from low-income countries.

Searches covered studies published only through May 2021; at the September 2026 review this evidence map is more than five years out of date. Community-level outcomes and process measures are rarely reported. Included work does not assess affordability or lack of accessibility, and adverse effects are seldom reported.

Searches covered studies published only through May 2021; at the September 2026 review this evidence map is more than five years out of date. More than 70% of the included systematic reviews were rated critically low quality.

limitations.text: Searches extended through May 2021; this is not a current exhaustive map.
A map describes coverage and gaps, not a pooled intervention effect.

claims.text: Among 18 interviewees selected because they already had an established chatbot friendship, participants described accepting, understanding, and nonjudgmental responses as factors in relationship development; these are reported perceptions, not proven clinical benefits.
population_scope: 18 participants who had already developed a friendship with Replika

claims.text: Effects on users’ wider social context were mixed, and participants reported stigma associated with human–chatbot relationships.

Delivering Cognitive Behavior Therapy to Young Adults With Symptoms of Depression and Anxiety Using a Fully Automated Conversational Agent (Woebot): A Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR Publications, 2017-06-06. DOI 10.2196/mental.7785. This record contains new paraphrases, not verbatim full text.

references.locator: Abstract: Methods and Results; author affiliations and study limitations

claims.text: Commercial-conflict disclosure: Alison Darcy was affiliated with Woebot Labs. In this unblinded two-week randomized study of 70 university-community young adults, with 17% missing follow-up, the Woebot arm showed a greater PHQ-9 reduction than the information-only control. This does not support a long-term or older-adult conclusion.
population_scope: Adults aged 18–28 recruited from a university community

claims.text: Anxiety decreased in both groups in the completer analysis; this does not establish a differential anxiety benefit for Woebot.
population_scope: Adults aged 18–28 recruited from a university community

limitations.text: Short follow-up, unblinded allocation and a university sample limit transferability to older adults.
Seventeen percent did not provide follow-up data; a study author was affiliated with Woebot Labs.

references.locator: Abstract: Methods and Results; author affiliations and study limitations

claims.text: Commercial-conflict disclosure: several authors were affiliated with Youper. Among 4517 paying users, anxiety and depression scores fell during the first two weeks; anxiety gains persisted over the next two weeks while depression scores rose slightly. This must not be summarized as uniform overall improvement.
population_scope: Paying Youper users who consented to research use of their data

claims.text: Week-four retention was 1927 of 4517 users (42.66%). Retention and app ratings do not establish clinical effectiveness.
population_scope: Paying Youper users who consented to research use of their data

limitations.text: Paying-user selection, attrition and lack of randomized comparison limit causal conclusions.
Several authors were affiliated with Youper; older-adult applicability requires separate assessment.
